Mini-batch stochastic gradient descent ● Mini-batch stochastic gradient descent (mini- batch SGD) is a compromise between full-batch and SGD. ● For N number of data points, the batch size can be any number greater than 1 and less than N. ● The model chooses the examples included in each batch at random, averages their gradients, and then updates the weights and bias once per iteration. When training a model, you might think that noise is an undesirable characteristic that should be eliminated. However, a certain amount of noise can be a good thing. Epochs ●During training, an epoch means that the model has processed every example in the training set once. For instance, a training set with 1000 examples and a mini-batch size of 100 examples, it will take the model 10 iterations to complete one epoch. ●Training typically requires many epochs and the system needs to process every example in the training set multiple times. ●The number of epochs is a hyperparameter that you need to set before the model begins training. ●In many cases, you’ll need to experiment with how many epochs it takes for the model to converge. ●In general, more epochs produces a better model, but also takes more time to train. Introduction • Naive Bayes is a supervised machine learning algorithm used mainly for classification tasks. • It is based on Bayes' Theorem — a rule that calculates the probability of an event based on prior knowledge of conditions related to the event. • Uses probability to classify data. Picks the class with the higher probability. • "Naive": Because it naively assumes feature independence, even though, in reality, features might be related. (e.g., "win" and "prize" are treated as unrelated). • "Bayes": Because it is based on Bayes’ Theorem, developed by mathematician Thomas Bayes. 3

Topic 9: Supervised Learning Modelling And Evaluation: Classification Using Naïve Bayes • Introduction to Naïve Bayes Classification • Application & Types of Naïve Bayes • Advantages and Disadvantages of Naïve Bayes Classifier 26

Advantages 1. Simple and Easy to Implement ∙ Requires relatively short training time compared to more complex algorithms. 2. Computationally Efficient ∙ Has a very low computation cost and requires fewer computational resources. ∙ Scales well with data, even for large datasets. ∙ Has low storage requirements. 3. Performs Well with Limited Training Data ∙ Effective even with small amounts of training data. ∙ Requires less data for training compared to other models like logistic regression or decision trees. 27

Advantages 4. Handles High-Dimensional Data ∙ Performs well with a large number of features. ∙ Particularly effective for use cases like document classification, where data is high- dimensional. 5. Strong Performance Despite Independence Assumption ∙ Despite assuming feature independence, it often delivers surprisingly accurate results. ∙ When the independence assumption holds, it can outperform models like logistic regression and decision trees. 6. Works Well with Categorical Features ∙ Particularly effective when the input features are categorical. ∙ Performs better with discrete variables compared to continuous variables. 28

Advantages 7. Can Handle Numerical Features ∙ Can work with numerical features by assuming they follow a normal (Gaussian) distribution — although this is a strong assumption. 8. Versatility ∙ Can be used for both binary and multi-class prediction problems. ∙ Successfully applied across various fields, especially in text analytics and document classification. 9. Ease of Interpretation ∙ Provides clear insight into how each feature contributes to the prediction through conditional probabilities. 29

Disadvantages 1. Strong Independence Assumption ∙ Assumes that all features are independent, which is often unrealistic in real-world data. ∙ In practice, predictors are often correlated (e.g., the presence of "snow" and "cold" are related in text data), violating the independence assumption and possibly leading to incorrect classifications. 2. Zero Frequency Problem ∙ If a categorical variable value in the test set was not observed in the training data, the model assigns zero probability to the entire prediction. ∙ This is known as the "Zero Frequency" or "Zero Probability" problem. 30

Disadvantages 3. Sensitivity to Irrelevant Features ∙ Naïve Bayes can be affected by irrelevant features or noise in the data, potentially impacting its accuracy. 4. Poor Probability Estimates ∙ Naïve Bayes is considered a bad estimator of class probabilities. 5. Performance on Numerical Data ∙ Naïve Bayes tends to perform better on categorical data. ∙ For numerical features, it assumes a normal (Gaussian) distribution, which may not always be valid and could affect performance. 31

How is a Missing Value Represented in a Dataset? 1. NaN (Not a Number): In many programming languages and data analysis tools, missing values are represented as NaN. This is the default for libraries like Pandas in Python. 2. NULL or None: In databases and some programming languages, missing values are often represented as NULL or None. For instance, in SQL databases, a missing value is typically recorded as NULL. 3. Empty Strings: Sometimes, missing values are denoted by empty strings (""). This is common in text-based data or CSV files where a field might be left blank. 4. Special Indicators: Datasets might use specific indicators like -999, 9999, or other unlikely values to signify missing data. This is often seen in older datasets or specific industries where such conventions were established. 5. Blanks or Spaces: In some cases, particularly in fixed-width text files, missing values might be represented by spaces or blank fields. 10

Missing Completely At Random VS Missing At Random Missing Not At Random

Missing Completely At Random (MCAR) MCAR occurs when the probability of data being missing is uniform across all observations. There is no relationship between the missingness of data and any other observed or unobserved data within the dataset. This type of missing data is purely random and lacks any discernible pattern. Example: In a survey about library books, some overdue book values in the dataset are missing due to human error in recording. 13

Missing At Random (MAR) MAR data occurs when the probability of data being missing depends only on the observed data and not on the missing data itself. In other words, the missingness can be explained by variables for which you have complete information. There is a pattern in the missing values, but this pattern can be explained by other observed variables. Example: In a survey, ‘Age’ values might be missing for those who did not disclose their ‘Gender’. Here, the missingness of ‘Age’ depends on ‘Gender’, but the missing ‘Age’ values are random among those who did not disclose their ‘Gender’. 14

Missing Not At Random (MNAR) MNAR occurs when the missingness of data is related to the unobserved data itself, which is not included in the dataset. This type of missing data has a specific pattern that cannot be explained by observed variables. Example: In a survey about library books, people with more overdue books might be less likely to respond to the survey. Thus, the number of overdue books is missing and depends on the number of books overdue. 15

VLOOKUP()- Fill missing values from another dataset Function of VLOOKUP in Excel VLOOKUP() (Vertical Lookup) is a function in Excel used to search for a value in one column and return a corresponding value from another column in the same row. It is commonly used to retrieve information from large datasets, such as product prices, employee details, or student grades. =VLOOKUP(lookup_value, table_array, col_index_num, [range_lookup]) Arguments: 1. lookup_value – The value you want to search for (e.g., Product ID, Employee ID). 2. table_array – The range of data containing the lookup value and the value to return. 3. col_index_num – The column number (starting from 1) from which to return the result. 4. [range_lookup] – (Optional) • TRUE (Approximate match) – If an exact match is not found, it returns the closest lower value. • FALSE (Exact match) – Only returns a result if an exact match is found. 56

Z-Score (Standard Deviation) • A Z-Score (also known as a standard score) tells you how far a data point is from the mean (average) of a dataset, in terms of standard deviations. • Z-scores help: a. Understand how unusual a value is b. Detect outliers c. Standardize values for comparison Formula: Z-score= (X−μ) σ Where: •X = your data point •μ = the mean (average) •σ = the standard deviation 26 UTM Faculty of Artificial Intelligence UNIVERSITI TEKNOLOGI MALAYSIA

Example Let's say we have test scores: [70, 75, 80, 85, 90] • Mean (μ) = 80 • Standard Deviation (σ) ≈ 7.91 Now, we calculate the Z-score for 90: Z=(90−80) 7.91 ≈1.26 This means 90 is 1.26 standard deviations above the average. IQR Method (Interquartile Range) • Quartiles break the date set into four equal portions. • The first quartile, or the Q1 , is the point below 25% of the data. • The second quartile, also known as the median or Q2 , is the midpoint of the data. • The third quartile, or Q3 , is the point where 75% of the data is below it. • Sitting between Q1 and Q3 , the interquartile range (IQR = Q3 - Q1 ) is used in calculating outliers. SAIA 2143 - 8 - Description: This dataset contains real-time weather and air quality data from 211 different countries. 1. Location & Time These columns tell us where and when the weather data was recorded. • country: The name of the country (e.g., "Malaysia", "Japan", "USA"). • location_name: The specific city or region within that country (e.g., "Kuala Lumpur", "Tokyo"). • latitude: The geographic coordinate specifying North/South location. • longitude: The geographic coordinate specifying East/West location. • timezone: The local time zone of the location (e.g., "Asia/Kuala_Lumpur"). • last_updated: The exact date and time the weather was recorded (YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM). • last_updated_epoch: The time recorded in "Unix format" (total seconds since Jan 1, 1970). Mainly used by computers for sorting. 2. Temperature & Weather Condition These columns describe how hot/cold it is and what the sky looks like. • temperature_celsius: The current air temperature in degrees Celsius (°C). • temperature_fahrenheit: The current air temperature in degrees Fahrenheit (°F). • feels_like_celsius: The "Real Feel" temperature. This accounts for humidity and wind (e.g., it might be 30°C but "feel like" 35°C due to humidity). • feels_like_fahrenheit: The "Real Feel" temperature in Fahrenheit. • condition_text: A text description of the weather (e.g., "Sunny", "Partly Cloudy", "Heavy Rain"). • uv_index: A number from 1-11+ measuring the strength of sunburn-causing ultraviolet radiation. o 1-2 (Low), 11+ (Extreme). 3. Wind & Atmosphere These columns describe the movement of air and storm conditions. • wind_kph: Wind speed in Kilometers per Hour (km/h). • wind_mph: Wind speed in Miles per Hour (mph). • wind_degree: The direction the wind is coming from, measured in degrees (0° = North, 90° = East). • wind_direction: The compass direction of the wind (e.g., "N", "SW", "ENE"). • gust_kph: The speed of sudden, brief bursts of wind (gusts) in km/h. • gust_mph: The speed of wind gusts in mph. • pressure_mb: Atmospheric pressure in millibars. Lower pressure often indicates a storm is coming. • pressure_in: Atmospheric pressure in inches of mercury (standard US measurement).

SAIA 2143 4. Rain, Visibility & Clouds These columns describe moisture and clarity. - 9 - • precip_mm: The amount of precipitation (rain/snow) that has fallen recently, in millimeters. • precip_in: The amount of precipitation in inches. • humidity: The percentage (%) of moisture in the air. 100% usually means rain or fog. • cloud: Cloud cover percentage (0% = Clear Sky, 100% = Totally Overcast). • visibility_km: How far you can see clearly, in kilometers. Lower numbers mean fog or haze. • visibility_miles: How far you can see clearly, in miles. 5. Air Quality (Pollution) These columns measure pollutants in the air. Higher numbers = Worse air quality. • air_quality_PM2.5: Tiny particles (dust/smoke) small enough to enter the lungs. This is a key measure of pollution. • air_quality_PM10: Larger dust/smoke particles. • air_quality_Carbon_Monoxide: Level of CO gas (often from cars/exhaust). • air_quality_Ozone: Level of Ozone gas (O3). • air_quality_Nitrogen_dioxide: Level of NO2 (often from burning fuel). • air_quality_Sulphur_dioxide: Level of SO2 (often from factories). • air_quality_us-epa-index: A summary score from 1 (Good) to 6 (Hazardous) used by the US EPA. • air_quality_gb-defra-index: A summary score from 1 (Low) to 10 (Very High) used by the UK government. 6. Astronomy (Sun & Moon) These columns track the cycle of the day and night. • sunrise: The time the sun rises (e.g., "06:30 AM"). • sunset: The time the sun sets (e.g., "07:15 PM"). • moonrise: The time the moon rises. • moonset: The time the moon sets. • moon_phase: The shape of the moon (e.g., "Full Moon", "Waxing Crescent"). moon_illumination: The percentage of the moon's face that is lit up (0% = New Moon, 100% = Full Moon).
